pure-announcement.rationale: This is Cribl's definitional/educational explainer of the observability-pipeline pattern, not a launch or release note; the product pitch appears only as a closing section, not the substance.

duplicate.rationale: telemetry-collector-pipeline covers the OTel Collector's technical receiver/processor/exporter architecture and adoption cost; this note's central idea — that decoupling sources from destinations makes whoever operates the pipeline the control point over collection, normalization and routing, with concrete leverage (multi-destination fan-out, volume/cost control, on-demand granularity) — is not present there.

unfalsifiable.rationale: The note is itself a primary source (Cribl's own explainer, attributing the coined term to Tyler Treat) and names a reproducible reference architecture (schema normalization, routing, stream processing, centralized state) a reader could build from open-source components, per its own FAQ.

durability.rationale: The core claim — a pipeline layer between sources and destinations gives its operator control over what is collected, how it's normalized, and where it's routed — is an architectural pattern independent of Cribl's product, version numbers or pricing, and will still hold in twelve months.

actionability.rationale: Gives concrete decision guidance: when to consolidate collection agents, what a vendor-neutral reference architecture needs (schema normalization, routing, stream processing, centralized state), and why to route one source to multiple destinations rather than picking one — a builder can act on this directly.

atomicity.rationale: The three 'problems' the source walks through (agent fatigue, capacity anxiety, the foresight trap) are facets of one move — inserting a pipeline layer that decouples producers from consumers — so the core idea reduces to a single paragraph independent of the source's marketing framing.

proposed_concepts.title: Observability pipeline as a control point
proposed_concepts.definition: Because all telemetry passes through a pipeline layer inserted between sources and destinations, whoever operates that layer controls what data exists downstream: which sources are consolidated (collection), what common shape the data is forced into (normalization), and which destinations receive which subset (routing) — turning an architectural position into leverage over cost, vendor choice and visibility.
